Romanian Business News - ACTMedia :: Services | About us | Contact | RSS Home Daily Financial & banking Economic Companies Energy & Environment Council of Europe calls for strengthening of elderly care system in Romania and investigation of Dumbrava case The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, Michael O'Flaherty, published on Tuesday a letter addressed to Romanian Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan, following his visit to Romania from May 26 to 29, 2026, in which he makes a series of recommendations regarding the long-term care system for the elderly, the Strasbourg-based organization announced. The Commissioner welcomes progress in the reform of social services and the dedication of staff working in care centers for the elderly. At the same time, he expresses concern about several challenges, including the insufficient recognition of residents as full holders of rights, the shortage of services and the difficulties faced by vulnerable people in accessing care services. Michael O'Flaherty recommends further developing the care system to meet complex needs and ensure better integration of health and social services. As regards monitoring, the Commissioner recommends that inspections of care facilities should pay greater attention to the well-being and rights of residents, in addition to checking formal compliance with standards. He also stresses the need for adequate and sustainable funding so that service providers can provide care according to needs and to the appropriate standards. The Commissioner's visit to Romania focused on the human rights situation of older people living in long-term care facilities and is part of a wider effort on this issue in Council of Europe member states. During his visit, Michael O'Flaherty met with the Minister of Investments and European Projects and Acting Minister of Labour, Dragos Pislaru, representatives of the Ministries of Labour and Health, the Prosecutor General's Office, the Ombudswoman Renate Weber, representatives of the Romanian Institute for Human Rights and civil society. He also visited three long-term care centres in Bucharest and Voluntari, where he spoke with residents, employees and representatives of local authorities. In a letter to Prime Minister Bolojan after this visit, copied to the Acting Minister of Labour, Dragos Pislaru, the Commissioner warns that the lack of care services makes access to them more difficult, in the context of an ageing population and increasing care needs. According to the Commissioner, some of the most vulnerable people, including those living in poverty, with disabilities or mental health problems, often end up not receiving the necessary support due to the fragmentation of care systems. In this context, he recommends developing a system capable of responding to the complex needs of beneficiaries, instead of relying on rigid classifications. The official points out that inspections often focus on compliance with formal standards, without giving sufficient priority to the people at the heart of these requirements. He considers it useful to review inspection methods so that, alongside technical criteria, the actual respect for the rights and well-being of residents is also assessed. Concerns were also expressed during the visit about the adequacy and sustainability of financing long-term care services. The Commissioner recommends that national and European funds be allocated through clear and accessible procedures, so that service providers - mostly non-profit organisations - can continue to provide the necessary care, according to needs and to the required standards. The Commissioner draws attention to care centres operating without a license and calls for a thorough and independent investigation into the Dumbrava case. According to the letter, dated 10 July, this concerns the unlicensed care centre in the village of Dumbrava, Bihor county, which allegedly housed thousands of vulnerable people in abusive conditions and where over a thousand deaths were recorded. The authorities should apply licensing conditions more strictly, adopt the necessary legislative amendments and strengthen monitoring mechanisms, including by increasing support to the Ombudsman. The Commissioner also recommends the establishment of accessible channels through which residents can report problems and seek remedies, as well as support for non-governmental organizations that promote human rights and dignity. In the letter, Michael O'Flaherty welcomes the recent intervention of Directorate for Investigating Organised Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT) and the transfer of residents to hospitals and licensed care facilities. He also expresses concern that the situation in Dumbrava has persisted for so long, despite repeated warnings from civil society organisations and journalists, as well as the recommendations of the Ombudswoman. The Commissioner also notes that the public debate on DIICOT's intervention has become polarised and that individuals who have exposed these abuses have been targeted with hate messages online. He stresses that the proceedings in the Dumbrava case must be conducted with integrity and independence, and the circumstances, including those relating to the registered deaths, must be investigated in detail. At the same time, the Commissioner recommends the analysis and adoption of additional legal provisions, including in the criminal field, if necessary, to combat the operation of illegal centers. In conclusion, he encourages the Romanian authorities to establish clear procedures for reporting and investigating deaths in residential centers for the elderly, following the model of existing mechanisms for people with disabilities. ( Reuters: Alexander Ermochenko ) In short: Russian authorities have reported multiple cyber attacks on its voting systems as Russians vote in its parliamentary election. Voting in Russia's parliamentary election runs from September 18 to 20. What's next? The Kremlin is likely to cite the election result as evidence of widespread public support for Mr Putin's policies, in particular the invasion of Ukraine. abc.net.au/news/russia-reports-cyberattacks-during-election/107172738 Link copied Share Share article Russian authorities have reported multiple attacks on voting systems and communication lines across the country, as Russians head to the polls in a three-day parliamentary election. The online voting system in Moscow was subjected to a strong attack overnight, but the situation remains under control, the Interfax news agency cited the Central Election Commission's head as saying on Saturday. The attacks were continuing, but all were being successfully repelled, Ella Pamfilova said, according to state media. A banner of Mr Putin with a quote reading: "Today, our entire country is one team. And that is undoubtedly the reason for the success of all our endeavours." ( Reuters: Alexey Pavlishak ) Separately, Russia's digital ministry said it had registered a sabotage attempt on communication lines in the country's Far East, but that the attack had been thwarted and all communication had been restored, state media reported. President Vladimir Putin earlier accused Ukraine of trying to interfere with the vote, without providing evidence. Voting in Russia's parliamentary election runs from September 18 to 20. Election triggers diplomatic row with Moldova Russia's parliamentary election has triggered a diplomatic row with Moldova over plans to open polling stations for Russian nationals in the separatist Transnistria region. Moscow says 220,000 residents of pro-Russian Transnistria, a sliver of land which broke away from Moldova in 1990 at the end of Soviet rule, hold Russian passports and are entitled to vote on Sunday in the election for the State Duma. Moldova's pro-Western government says Russians may vote only in a single polling station in the Russian embassy in the capital Chisinau. It contests the 220,000 figure and opposes any polling station in Transnistria, where it has no control over procedures. Moldovan authorities this week denounced the Kremlin's 15 planned polling stations as "unacceptable and hostile". Putin's new incentives to recruit soldiers in Transnistria The Kremlin is trying to recruit more soldiers for its war in Ukraine but an analyst says at the rate of casualties, "Russia cannot replace recruits fast enough to keep the 'meat grinder' fed." Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova urged Moldova to drop its objections and halt actions that "run against democracy, international law and common sense". Moldovan Foreign Minister Mihail Popsoi told Moscow "not to interfere with Moldova's plans for peaceful reintegration" of the breakaway territory. Flags of Transnistria and Russia fly in a square in Moldova's breakaway region of Transnistria. ( Reuters: Vladislav Bachev ) Meanwhile, former Russian federal official Marat Kambolov was elected president of South Ossetia, a Russia-backed breakaway region of Georgia, in a vote Moscow hailed on Saturday as a sign of the territory's desire for closer ties with Moscow. Election shadowed by war The Kremlin is likely to cite the election result as evidence of widespread public support for Mr Putin's policies, in particular the invasion of Ukraine — Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II, now in its fifth year. Most anti-war candidates have been barred from participating. The second day of voting came after a New York Time report this week, citing two people close to the peace talks, that the White House is now considering signing business deals with Russia before it stops fighting in Ukraine. Democrats probe Trump Jr wedding parties Two lavish post-wedding parties for Donald Trump Jr and his wife, held in the Bahamas in May, were funded by Russian businessman Umar Kremlev, who has strong ties to President Vladimir Putin, according to a report by US media outlet ProPublica. "I don't know anything about such signals, and it would be strange to receive them, because we still hear exactly the opposite stance, namely, 'Let's agree on Ukraine and move forward, and everything else later,'" Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov told the RIA state news agency on Saturday. Also on Saturday, Poland said it conducted a preventative military air operation during Russian strikes on Ukraine — though concluded there was no violation of Polish airspace. Moldova said it suffered an "unacceptable" violation of its airspace, as it suspected an explosion near its capital to be caused by a drone "from Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine". Russian forces struck a Ukrainian cargo ship and a tanker located in the Black Sea and in one of Ukraine's ports, the Interfax news agency reported on Saturday, citing the Russian Defence Ministry.
